subject: Economics
description: Money supply, RBI instruments, scheduled banks, NPAs

questions.stem: The RESERVE BANK OF INDIA was established in the year:
questions.explanation: RBI was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934. Based on recommendations of the Hilton Young Commission (1926). Nationalised on 1 January 1949. Headquartered in Mumbai. First Indian Governor: C. D. Deshmukh (1943).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: The rate at which the RBI lends SHORT-TERM funds to commercial banks against government securities is called:

options.option_text: Bank Rate
Repo Rate
Reverse Repo Rate
SLR

questions.explanation: REPO (re-purchase) — banks borrow from RBI by selling G-Secs with agreement to repurchase. Reverse repo = opposite direction, RBI borrows from banks. Bank Rate — long-term lending rate by RBI (now ≈ MSF rate). SLR/CRR are reserve ratios, not lending rates.
questions.subject: Economics

options.option_text: % of bank's net demand and time liabilities kept as cash reserve with RBI
% of deposits banks lend at repo rate
Minimum ratio of NPA to total loans
Gold holding required by the central bank

questions.explanation: CRR = cash with RBI (no interest earned). SLR = proportion of NDTL held in safe liquid assets (gold, cash, approved securities) with the bank itself. Both are monetary-policy tools: higher CRR/SLR → less money to lend → tighter liquidity.

questions.stem: Match the MONETARY AGGREGATE with its components. A. M0. B. M1. C. M3. List-II: 1. Currency with public + demand deposits with banks + other deposits with RBI. 2. M1 + time deposits with banks (the 'broad money'). 3. Reserve Money = currency in circulation + bankers' deposits with RBI + other deposits with RBI.
questions.explanation: M0 = Reserve Money (narrowest). M1 = narrow money (currency + demand deposits). M2 = M1 + post office savings. M3 = broad money (most commonly quoted). M4 = M3 + all post-office deposits (broadest).

questions.stem: A 'scheduled' commercial bank in India is one that is included in the:

options.option_text: First Schedule of the Indian Constitution
Second Schedule of the RBI Act, 1934
Companies Act, 2013
Banking Regulation Act, 1949 annexure

questions.explanation: Section 42(6)(a) of the RBI Act — a scheduled bank has paid-up capital + reserves ≥ ₹5 lakh and satisfies RBI that its affairs are not conducted to the detriment of depositors. Scheduled banks are eligible for loans from RBI and automatic membership of clearing houses.

questions.stem: An NPA (Non-Performing Asset) in Indian banking is a loan for which interest/principal is overdue for:

options.option_text: 30 days
60 days
90 days
180 days

questions.explanation: RBI's prudential norms: a term loan is NPA if interest or principal instalment remains overdue > 90 days. Once classified NPA, bank must provision for it; prompt-corrective-action (PCA) framework kicks in if NPAs breach thresholds.

questions.stem: Consider the following statements about RBI. 1. It is the banker to the Government of India and issuer of currency. 2. It regulates foreign exchange under FEMA, 1999. 3. The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) sets the policy repo rate to achieve a flexible inflation target. 4. The target currently is headline CPI inflation of 4% within a ±2% tolerance band. Which are correct?

options.option_text: 1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3 only
2 and 4 only

questions.explanation: All four correct. MPC is 6-member (3 RBI + 3 government-appointed externals). Flexible inflation targeting framework was adopted in 2016. Target: 4% CPI inflation with tolerance band 2-6%.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requires banks to maintain a minimum fraction of their Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) in which of the following permissible forms?

options.option_text: Cash deposits held with Reserve Bank of India alone
Gold, cash, or RBI-approved government securities
Foreign exchange reserves and approved equity holdings
Fixed deposits placed with any scheduled commercial bank

questions.explanation: SLR mandates that banks park a prescribed share of NDTL in liquid assets: gold, cash in hand, or government and other approved securities. Option A is wrong because SLR assets are not restricted to RBI deposits — that is CRR. Options C and D name instruments that are not RBI-approved SLR-eligible assets.

questions.stem: Under the Marginal Standing Facility (MSF), scheduled commercial banks can borrow overnight from the RBI by pledging securities drawn specifically from which source?

options.option_text: Excess CRR balances maintained with the Reserve Bank of India
Securities held within the bank's own SLR portfolio quota
Foreign currency assets held in overseas NOSTRO accounts
Subordinated debt instruments previously issued to retail depositors

questions.explanation: MSF allows banks to borrow overnight by dipping into their SLR-eligible securities portfolio (up to 2% of NDTL), even if doing so temporarily breaches the SLR floor. This distinguishes MSF from the repo window, where only excess (non-SLR) securities are pledged. CRR balances (Option A) cannot be pledged under MSF.

questions.stem: As per RBI's Master Direction on Priority Sector Lending, what is the agriculture sub-target that domestic scheduled commercial banks must lend as a share of Adjusted Net Bank Credit (ANBC)?

options.option_text: 10% of ANBC, as prescribed under the Basel II framework norms
18% of ANBC, with 8% ring-fenced for small and marginal farmers
25% of ANBC, as mandated by the Ministry of Finance guidelines
40% of ANBC, which is the aggregate priority sector lending ceiling

questions.explanation: The agriculture-specific sub-target under Priority Sector Lending is 18% of ANBC, of which at least 8% must flow to small and marginal farmers. Option D (40%) is the overall PSL target across all categories — a common mix-up. 10% and 25% do not correspond to any agriculture PSL threshold.

questions.stem: Which of the following most accurately identifies a key regulatory distinction between a Non-Banking Financial Company (NBFC) and a scheduled commercial bank in India?

options.option_text: An NBFC can freely issue demand drafts and letters of credit
An NBFC can extend loans secured against movable and immovable assets
An NBFC cannot accept demand deposits repayable instantly on call
An NBFC is regulated exclusively by the Ministry of Finance alone

questions.explanation: The single sharpest legal distinction is that NBFCs cannot accept demand deposits (current/savings accounts withdrawable on demand). They may accept time deposits but are excluded from the payment and settlement system and deposit insurance (DICGC). Option A is wrong — NBFCs cannot issue demand drafts. Option D is wrong — RBI is the primary regulator of NBFCs, not the Finance Ministry.

questions.stem: In a 'reverse repo' transaction under the RBI's Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), which of the following correctly describes the mechanics of the operation?

options.option_text: RBI lends short-term funds to banks by buying their government securities
Banks park surplus cash with RBI by purchasing government securities temporarily
RBI provides emergency funds against SLR-ineligible collateral to banks
Banks borrow from RBI against pledge of their approved CRR surplus balances

questions.explanation: In a reverse repo, banks lend surplus funds to RBI: banks buy government securities from RBI with an agreement that RBI repurchases them — this absorbs excess liquidity from the system. Option A describes a plain repo (liquidity injection, not absorption). Option C describes the MSF/SLF window. RBI absorbs liquidity through reverse repos while injecting it through repos.

questions.stem: Under the revised RBI Prompt Corrective Action (PCA) framework effective January 2022, mandatory restrictions on a bank are triggered by breach of threshold limits on which combination of indicators?

options.option_text: CRAR or CET1, Net NPA ratio, and Tier 1 Leverage Ratio
Gross NPA ratio, Return on Equity, and Credit-Deposit Ratio
SLR shortfall, CRR deficit, and Priority Sector Lending gap
Repo Rate exposure, FOREX reserves, and Capital Conservation Buffer

questions.explanation: The 2021-revised PCA framework (effective 1 January 2022) uses three risk dimensions: capital (CRAR / CET1), asset quality (Net NPA ratio), and leverage (Tier 1 Leverage Ratio). Return on Assets — a parameter in the earlier framework — was removed in the 2021 revision; candidates who memorised the old framework are misled by its omission. Options B, C, and D mix in metrics that are not PCA trigger parameters.

questions.stem: The Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) of RBI comprises six members and decides the policy repo rate by majority vote. What happens constitutionally if the vote ends in a tie?

options.option_text: The Finance Minister casts the deciding vote as an ex-officio MPC member
The RBI Governor exercises a second casting vote to resolve the deadlock
The matter is referred to the RBI Central Board of Directors for resolution
The decision is deferred automatically to the next scheduled MPC meeting date

questions.explanation: Section 45ZI(8) of the RBI Act, 1934 explicitly provides that 'in the event of an equality of votes, the Governor shall have a second or casting vote.' The Finance Minister is not an MPC member (Option A is a common misconception — the government nominates three external members, but the Finance Minister sits outside the MPC). The Central Board has no MPC jurisdiction (Option C), and deferral is not a statutory resolution mechanism (Option D).
